events.title: Murder of Justin son of Germanus at Alexandria
events.summary: Justin, son of Justinian's cousin Germanus and the most experienced general of the dynasty, had been a rival candidate in 565. Justin II sent him to Alexandria as a quasi-exile and had him killed there in 566; Evagrius says his head was brought to the emperor and empress, who kicked it.
events.debate: Evagrius is hostile to Justin II; the head-kicking detail may be rhetorical.

events.title: Execution of the senators Aetherius and Addaeus
events.summary: Two senior senators, the curator Aetherius and the former prefect Addaeus, were accused of plotting to poison Justin II and executed in 566. Evagrius treats the charge as a pretext to remove survivors of Justinian's inner circle.

events.title: Justin II sends a relic of the True Cross to Radegund at Poitiers
events.summary: At the request of the Frankish ex-queen Radegund, Justin II and Sophia sent a fragment of the True Cross in a jewelled reliquary to her convent at Poitiers, which took the name Sainte-Croix. For its reception Venantius Fortunatus composed the hymns Vexilla regis prodeunt and Pange lingua, still sung in the Latin liturgy of Holy Week.
events.note: Fortunatus's poem In laudem Iustini et Sophiae thanks the imperial couple; the reliquary's identification with the surviving Poitiers staurotheke is plausible but not certain.

events.title: Tiberius defeated by the Avars
events.summary: As comes excubitorum, the future Tiberius II led an army against the Avars on the lower Danube and was beaten around 570-571. The defeat forced Justin II, who had haughtily refused Avar subsidies in 565, to accept a truce, while the khagan Bayan turned to the Gepid inheritance and Sirmium.

battle.significance: Showed the limits of Justin II's refusal to pay the Avars.

events.debate: Date (570 or 571) and location are uncertain; Menander's fragments give the diplomatic context.

events.title: Abraha's expedition against Mecca: the 'Year of the Elephant'
events.summary: Muslim tradition holds that Abraha, the Aksumite viceroy of Yemen, marched on Mecca with an elephant to destroy the Kaaba, and that his army was destroyed by birds pelting stones (Qur'an 105) in the year of Muhammad's birth, conventionally 570. Abraha's own Murayghan inscription (Ry 506) records a campaign deep into central Arabia in 552.
events.debate: Many scholars date the expedition c. 552 or the 560s and doubt the synchronism with Muhammad's birth, which may be a later symbolic construction.

events.title: Sasanian conquest of Yemen
events.summary: Khosrow I sent a small force under the general Wahriz, reputedly drawn from prisoners, to help the Himyarite prince Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan expel the Aksumites. The Ethiopian dynasty of Abraha's sons fell and Yemen became a Persian dependency ruled by a marzban until the 620s, giving Persia control of the southern Red Sea and the incense route.
events.debate: Dated anywhere from c. 570 to 575; the story of the prisoner army is Arabic tradition.

events.title: Plague in Italy and Gaul
events.summary: A further wave of the bubonic plague swept northern Italy and Gaul around 570-571. Marius of Avenches records a great mortality of men and cattle; Gregory of Tours describes the inguinal plague at Clermont, where on one Sunday 300 bodies were counted in the basilica of St Peter. Paul the Deacon's picture of empty villas and unharvested fields in Liguria belongs to these years.

events.title: Justin II turns on the miaphysites
events.summary: After his compromise edict, sometimes called the second Henotikon, failed to win over the anti-Chalcedonians, Justin II and Patriarch John Scholasticus enforced communion from 571: miaphysite clergy were reordained or imprisoned and monasteries in the capital emptied. John of Ephesus, himself jailed, wrote much of his Ecclesiastical History in prison as a record of the persecution.

events.title: Lombard duchies of Spoleto and Benevento founded
events.summary: Lombard war bands moving south of Roman-held Ravenna and Rome set up autonomous duchies around Spoleto, under Faroald, and Benevento, under Zotto, in the 570s. They cut the Via Flaminia between Rome and Ravenna and would remain largely independent of the kings at Pavia for two centuries.
events.debate: Foundation dates are inferred; Paul gives Zotto a twenty-year reign ending c. 591, suggesting 571, but some prefer 576.

events.title: Leovigild takes Asidona from the Romans
events.summary: John of Biclaro says Leovigild seized the strongly fortified city of Asidona (Medina Sidonia) by night through the treachery of a certain Framidaneus, killed its Roman garrison and restored it to Gothic rule. It was the first major Visigothic gain against Justinian's province of Spania.

battle.significance: Opened Leovigild's reconquest of southern Spain.

events.title: Leovigild takes Córdoba
events.summary: Córdoba, which had defied the Gothic kings since the 550s and had defeated Agila, fell to a night attack by Leovigild in 572. John of Biclaro calls it 'long rebellious against the Goths'; Leovigild then took many towns and forts in the region, killing many peasants (rustici).
events.debate: Whether Córdoba was under Roman control or an autonomous Hispano-Roman city is debated.

events.title: Failed Roman siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Justin II's cousin Marcian besieged Nisibis in spring 573. Suspecting slackness, Justin replaced him with Acacius Archelaus, who removed him in front of the troops; when Khosrow I approached in person, the leaderless besiegers burned their siege engines and fled. The disaster opened the way to the Persian siege of Dara.

battle.significance: Rout that preceded the loss of Dara.

events.title: Adarmahan sacks Apamea
events.summary: While Khosrow besieged Dara, his general Adarmahan with a raiding army crossed the Euphrates at Circesium, plundered northern Syria, burned the suburbs of Antioch and took Apamea, whose bishop and citizens had trusted to its relic of the True Cross. Evagrius, an Antiochene, saw the devastation; the captives were marched to Persia.

battle.significance: Deepest Persian raid into Syria since 540.

events.debate: John of Ephesus's figures for the captives are enormous and untrustworthy.

events.title: Madness of Justin II
events.summary: The loss of Dara broke Justin II. John of Ephesus describes the emperor hiding under beds, biting his attendants, and being pacified by organ music and by being pulled around in a little wagon. Sophia took control and in December 574 Justin, in a lucid moment, proclaimed Tiberius Caesar with a speech the sources quote as a confession of failure.

events.title: Sophia buys a truce with Persia
events.summary: Empress Sophia sent the physician Zacharias to Khosrow and bought a one-year truce for 45,000 solidi; it was later extended for three years at 30,000 a year but covered only Mesopotamia, leaving Armenia as an open war zone. The arrangement freed Roman forces to rebuild but confirmed the loss of Dara.

events.title: Murder of Cleph and the rule of the dukes
events.summary: Alboin's successor Cleph was murdered after eighteen months in 574. For ten years the Lombards elected no king; Paul the Deacon says some 35 dukes ruled their cities independently, killing or dispossessing Roman landowners and making the rest tributary for a third of their produce.
events.debate: The 'thirds' passage (PD 2.32) is central to the debate on Lombard settlement: expropriation versus tax-sharing.

events.title: Lombard and Saxon raids into Gaul defeated by Mummolus
events.summary: In the years after 569 Lombard war bands, and Saxons who had come to Italy with Alboin, crossed the Alps into Burgundian Gaul. The Gallo-Roman patrician Mummolus destroyed one army near Embrun and another at Mustiae Calmes, and the Saxons were forced back across the Rhône. The raids ended Lombard ambitions beyond the Alps.

battle.significance: Closed the Alpine passes to Lombard raiding.

events.title: Assassination of Sigibert I at Vitry
events.summary: In the civil war between Sigibert I of Austrasia and his brother Chilperic I, Sigibert had overrun Neustria and was raised on a shield at Vitry as king of Chilperic's people when two servants sent by Chilperic's queen Fredegund stabbed him with poisoned scramasaxes. The murder, revenge for Chilperic's killing of Brunhild's sister Galswintha, made the feud of Brunhild and Fredegund the axis of Frankish politics for forty years.

events.title: Baduarius defeated by the Lombards
events.summary: Justin II sent his son-in-law Baduarius, husband of Arabia, with an army to Italy. John of Biclaro records laconically that he was defeated by the Lombards and soon afterwards died. It was the last attempt by Constantinople to reconquer Lombard Italy with a field army; Tiberius II turned to bribing dukes and inviting the Franks.

battle.significance: Ended direct Roman offensives in Italy for a generation.

events.title: The Turks take Bosporus in the Crimea
events.summary: The envoy Valentinus reached the Western Turks in 576 to find the old ruler Istämi dead and his successor Turxanthus enraged that Tiberius had received the fleeing Avars, whom the Turks counted as runaway slaves. Turxanthus, putting ten fingers in his mouth to mock Roman duplicity, sent an army that captured the Roman city of Bosporus (Kerch).

battle.significance: Rupture of the Turkish alliance; the Turks reached the Black Sea coast.

events.title: Justinian son of Germanus defeated in Armenia
events.summary: After the Roman victory at Melitene (576), the magister militum per Orientem Justinian, son of Germanus, wintered in Persarmenia but was defeated in 577 by the Persian general Tamkhosrow. He was recalled and replaced by Maurice, then comes excubitorum.

battle.significance: Brought Maurice to the eastern command.

events.title: Eutychius restored; his debate with Gregory on the resurrection body
events.summary: Deposed by Justinian in 565 for resisting aphthartodocetism, Patriarch Eutychius returned from exile in 577. He taught that resurrected bodies would be impalpable, 'finer than air', and was opposed by the papal apocrisiarius Gregory, the future pope, in a debate before Tiberius II, who ordered Eutychius's treatise burned. Gregory retold the dispute in his Moralia on Job.

events.title: Lombards destroy Monte Cassino
events.summary: Lombards of the duchy of Benevento under Zotto attacked Benedict's monastery at night and destroyed it. The monks escaped to Rome, according to Paul the Deacon carrying Benedict's autograph Rule, a measure of bread and a measure of wine. Gregory's Dialogues present the destruction as foretold by Benedict. The site lay abandoned until c. 717.
events.debate: The date is given variously as 577, 581, 584 or 589.

events.title: Maurice invades Arzanene
events.summary: As new magister militum per Orientem, Maurice answered a Persian raid on Roman Mesopotamia by invading Arzanene east of the Tigris in 578, taking the fortress of Aphumon and others and deporting some 10,000 captives, who were resettled on Cyprus. He then raided as far as Corduene, demonstrating that Roman armies could carry the war into Persian territory.

events.title: Leovigild founds Reccopolis
events.summary: Having pacified his kingdom, Leovigild founded a city in Celtiberia named after his son Reccared, the first new city founded in western Europe since Roman times. Excavations at Zorita de los Canes have revealed a palace complex, a church and a street of shops behind an imposing wall, and a mint struck coins there.

events.title: Romans ferry the Avars across the Danube against the Slavs
events.summary: Unable to defend Thrace against Slav raiders while fighting Persia, Tiberius invited the khagan Bayan to attack the Sclaveni in their own lands. John, prefect of Illyricum, transported 60,000 Avar horsemen down the Danube on Roman ships and across it; Bayan ravaged the territory of the Slav leader Daurentius, who had reputedly killed an Avar envoy.

events.title: Gennadius defeats the Moorish king Garmul
events.summary: John of Biclaro records that the magister militum Gennadius ravaged the Moors in Africa and killed in battle the very powerful king Garmul, who had already killed three Roman commanders. Gennadius later appears as the first attested exarch of Africa.

battle.significance: Stabilised Roman Africa for a generation.

events.title: Death of Khosrow I; accession of Hormizd IV
events.summary: Khosrow I Anushirvan died in early 579 after 48 years on the throne, while peace talks were under way. His son Hormizd IV, a ruler later remembered for favouring the peasants and clashing with the great nobles and priests, broke off negotiations and refused to restore Dara.

events.title: Revolt of Hermenegild
events.summary: Leovigild's elder son Hermenegild, governing Baetica from Seville and married to the Catholic Frankish princess Ingund, converted to Catholicism under Leander of Seville and rebelled in 579, seeking help from the Romans of Spania and the Suebi. Leovigild took Seville in 584 after diverting the Guadalquivir, captured his son at Córdoba, and he was killed at Tarragona in 585. Gregory the Great later honoured him as a martyr.
events.debate: Spanish sources (John of Biclaro, Isidore) treat him as a rebel and say nothing of religion; the martyr image comes from Gregory.

events.title: Maurice and al-Mundhir's expedition toward Ctesiphon
events.summary: In 581 Maurice and the Ghassanid king al-Mundhir marched down the Euphrates with a river fleet intending to strike at Ctesiphon, but found the bridge at the frontier destroyed and Adarmahan raiding Osrhoene behind them. The fiasco led to bitter recriminations, with Maurice accusing al-Mundhir of betraying the plan to the Persians.

events.title: Arrest of the Ghassanid king al-Mundhir
events.summary: Suspected of treachery, al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith, the Miaphysite supreme phylarch who had defeated the Lakhmids repeatedly, was arrested in 582 by the curator Magnus at the consecration of a church at Huwwarin and exiled to Sicily. His son al-Nu'man rebelled, was in turn arrested (584), and the Ghassanid federation broke into some fifteen rival groups, weakening Rome's desert shield half a century before the Arab conquests.

events.title: Battle of Constantina
events.summary: In June 582 Maurice met a Persian invasion of Mesopotamia under Tamkhosrow and Adarmahan before Constantina (Tella) and won a clear victory in which Tamkhosrow was killed. Weeks later Tiberius II, dying, made Maurice Caesar and married him to his daughter Constantina.

battle.significance: Secured Maurice's succession.

events.title: Avars take Singidunum, Viminacium and Anchialus
events.summary: When Maurice refused Bayan's demand for an extra 20,000 solidi on top of the 80,000 paid annually, the Avars surprised Singidunum while its people were harvesting, then took Viminacium and Augustae and swept to Anchialus on the Black Sea, where Bayan spared the empress's warm baths. Peace was restored for an annual payment of 100,000 solidi, but Slavs then raided to the Long Walls.

events.title: Lombards restore the kingship: Authari
events.summary: Under pressure from Frankish and Roman attacks, the Lombard dukes elected Cleph's son Authari king in 584 and each gave half his substance to endow the royal fisc. Authari took the Roman name Flavius, used by later Lombard kings, and Paul the Deacon describes his reign as an idyll of peace without violence or plotting.

events.title: Murder of Chilperic I
events.summary: Chilperic I of Neustria was stabbed to death returning from a hunt at his villa of Chelles near Paris in autumn 584. Gregory of Tours, whom he had once tried for slander, calls him 'the Nero and Herod of our time', mocking his Latin verse and his attempt to add letters to the alphabet. His four-month-old son Chlothar II survived under Fredegund's protection.

events.title: Arrest of al-Nu'man and the break-up of the Ghassanid federation
events.summary: Al-Mundhir's son al-Nu'man, who had raided Roman territory in revenge for his father's exile, was lured to Constantinople and arrested in 584. John of Ephesus says the Arab federation split into fifteen factions, many joining the Persians; Rome never recreated a single supreme phylarchate.

events.title: The Gundovald affair
events.summary: Gundovald, who claimed to be a son of Chlothar I and had lived in Constantinople, landed at Marseille in 582 with imperial money, was raised on a shield at Brive in late 584 and won over much of Aquitaine. Besieged by Guntram's army in the hilltop town of Convenae (Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges) in 585, he was betrayed by his ally Mummolus and killed; the town was sacked. Gregory of Tours suspected Byzantine sponsorship.

battle.significance: Last Byzantine-backed pretender in Gaul.

events.title: Leovigild annexes the Suebic kingdom
events.summary: After Audeca usurped the Suebic throne from the young Eboric, Leovigild invaded Gallaecia in 585, captured Audeca, made him a cleric and annexed the kingdom of the Suebi, which had existed since 409. A brief rising under Malaric was crushed. The Visigoths now held all Iberia except the Basque lands and the Roman coast.

events.title: Siege of Chlomaron
events.summary: Following his victory at Solachon, Philippicus invaded Arzanene and besieged the fortress of Chlomaron. When a Persian relief army appeared he lost his nerve and retreated in disorder by night, abandoning much of the campaign's gains. Theophylact's account is one of the frankest descriptions of a Roman command collapse.

battle.significance: Squandered the advantage won at Solachon.

events.title: Comentiolus's Haemus campaign: 'torna, torna, fratre'
events.summary: During a night march against the Avars in the Haemus mountains in 587, a pack animal shed its load and a soldier called to its driver in the local Latin vernacular 'torna, torna, fratre' (turn back, brother). The cry was taken as an order to retreat and both the Roman army of Comentiolus and the Avars it was stalking fled in panic. The phrase is prized as one of the earliest records of Balkan Romance.

battle.significance: Famous for its linguistic evidence.

events.title: Reccared converts to Catholicism
events.summary: Ten months after succeeding Leovigild (586), Reccared privately accepted Nicene Christianity in early 587 and persuaded many Arian bishops and nobles to follow. Arian conspiracies at Mérida, in Septimania and at court, including one involving Leovigild's widow Goiswintha, were suppressed before the public abjuration at the Third Council of Toledo (589).

events.title: Treaty of Andelot
events.summary: On 28 November 587 Guntram of Burgundy, his nephew Childebert II of Austrasia and Childebert's mother Brunhild agreed at Andelot to divide disputed cities, guarantee Brunhild's lands, and make Childebert Guntram's heir. Gregory of Tours, who helped negotiate it, copied the full text into his Histories, a rare surviving Merovingian treaty.

events.title: The mutinous eastern army defeats the Persians near Martyropolis
events.summary: Even while in mutiny against Maurice's pay cut and his general Priscus, the eastern army under its elected leader Germanus beat a Persian invasion near Martyropolis in 588, killing the commander Maruzas and sending his head and captured standards to the emperor as proof of loyalty to the empire, if not to its officers.

battle.significance: Paved the way for reconciliation of the army in 589.

events.title: Bahram Chobin defeats the Turks
events.summary: A Turkic invasion of Khurasan was crushed by the Persian general Bahram Chobin, probably near Herat, in 588; the Turkic ruler, called Shaba or Sabeh in Persian tradition, was killed. Persian sources inflate the enemy to 300,000. The victory made Bahram a hero and gave him the prestige to rebel after Hormizd IV humiliated him for a later defeat by the Romans.

battle.significance: Created the war hero who would usurp the throne in 590.

events.title: Martyropolis betrayed to the Persians
events.summary: A Roman officer named Sittas betrayed Martyropolis to the Persians in 589 by bringing in Persian soldiers disguised as deserters. Roman sieges under Philippicus and then Comentiolus failed against a reinforced garrison; the city was handed back only through Khosrow II's restoration treaty in 591.

battle.significance: Strategic city lost by treachery and regained by diplomacy.

events.title: Battle of Sisarbanon
events.summary: In autumn 589 Comentiolus defeated a Persian army near Nisibis at Sisarbanon (Sisauranon). Theophylact says Comentiolus fled at the crisis but Heraclius the Elder, father of the future emperor, rallied the troops; the Persian general was killed and the Romans then took the fort of Akbas.

battle.significance: Contributed to the crisis that toppled Hormizd IV.

events.title: Battle of Carcassonne
events.summary: Guntram's Franks invaded Visigothic Septimania in 589 and were routed near Carcassonne by Claudius, dux of Lusitania. Isidore boasts that 300 Goths beat 60,000 Franks; John of Biclaro calls it the greatest Gothic victory in Spain. It secured Septimania for the Visigoths until the Arab conquest.

battle.significance: Confirmed Gothic Septimania.

events.title: Plague in Rome and the sevenfold litany
events.summary: After the Tiber flooded in late 589, plague struck Rome; Pope Pelagius II died on 7 February 590. The deacon Gregory, elected to succeed him, organised a sevenfold procession of clergy, monks, nuns, children, laymen, widows and married women converging on Santa Maria Maggiore; Gregory of Tours heard that eighty people dropped dead during it. The legend of Michael sheathing his sword over Hadrian's mausoleum, hence Castel Sant'Angelo, is medieval.

events.title: Frankish-Roman offensive against the Lombards
events.summary: Financed by Maurice, Childebert II sent twenty dukes into Italy in 590 while the exarch Romanus advanced from Ravenna, recovering Modena, Altinum and Mantua. The Franks, ravaged by dysentery and suspicious of Roman delays, made a separate truce and withdrew; letters of Romanus to Childebert in the Epistolae Austrasicae preserve the coalition's frustrations.

events.title: Columbanus founds Luxeuil
events.summary: The Irish monk Columbanus from Bangor arrived in Gaul with twelve companions around 590 and, with the support of the Burgundian king, founded monasteries at Annegray and then Luxeuil in the ruins of a Roman spa in the Vosges. His harsh Rule and Irish penitential practice inspired dozens of foundations across Francia in the seventh century.

events.title: John of Biclaro writes his Chronicle
events.summary: John, a Goth from Scallabis (Santarém) who had studied seventeen years in Constantinople, was exiled to Barcelona by the Arian Leovigild, founded a monastery at Biclaro and became bishop of Gerona. His chronicle, continuing Victor of Tunnuna from 567 to 590, is the main source for Leovigild and Reccared and is dated by both imperial and Gothic regnal years.

events.title: Deposition and murder of Hormizd IV
events.summary: With Bahram Chobin marching on Ctesiphon, the brothers Vistahm and Vinduyih (Bindoe), Hormizd's brothers-in-law, staged a palace coup in February 590, blinded the king and proclaimed his son Khosrow II; Hormizd was killed soon after. Khosrow's complicity was later debated, but Bahram used it as justification for his own claim.

events.title: Death of Authari; Agilulf marries Theodelinda
events.summary: Authari died at Pavia on 5 September 590, perhaps poisoned. The Lombards allowed his Bavarian Catholic widow Theodelinda to choose the next king; she married Agilulf, duke of Turin, who was proclaimed in November 590 and recognised at Milan in May 591.

events.title: The exarchate of Africa
events.summary: By 591 the governor of Roman Africa combined civil and military power with the title exarch, first attested for Gennadius in Gregory the Great's letters. Like Ravenna, Carthage became a semi-autonomous military command; in 608 the exarch Heraclius the Elder launched from it the revolt that put his son on the throne.
events.debate: The exarchate may have been created earlier by Maurice (c. 585); 591 is the first attestation.

events.title: Khosrow II's dedications to St Sergius at Resafa
events.summary: Restored by Roman arms, Khosrow II sent votive gifts to the shrine of St Sergius at Sergiopolis: a gold cross for the victory over Bahram, and later offerings in thanks for the pregnancy of his Christian wife Shirin. Evagrius quotes the Greek texts of the dedicatory inscriptions, in which the Zoroastrian King of Kings addresses the saint directly.

events.title: Exarch Romanus reopens the Rome-Ravenna corridor
events.summary: The exarch Romanus retook Sutri, Bomarzo, Orte, Todi, Amelia, Perugia and Luceoli from the Lombards around 592, securing the route along the Via Amerina that became the spine of the Byzantine duchy of Perugia linking Rome to Ravenna. Agilulf retook Perugia in 593 and marched on Rome.

events.title: Death of Guntram
events.summary: Guntram, king of Burgundy since 561 and the most pious of Chlothar I's sons, died on 28 March 592; under the Treaty of Andelot his kingdom passed to Childebert II. Popular devotion soon venerated him as a saint, despite Gregory of Tours's record of his executions.

events.title: Gregory the Great's Dialogues
events.summary: In 593-594 Gregory wrote four books of Dialogues on the miracles of the Italian fathers in conversation with his deacon Peter. Book 2, devoted entirely to Benedict of Nursia, is the only life of Benedict and made his Rule famous. Book 4 on the afterlife became a foundation of the medieval doctrine of purgatory.
events.debate: Francis Clark argued the Dialogues were a later forgery; most scholars reject this.

events.title: Peter's campaign beyond the Danube
events.summary: Maurice replaced Priscus with his own brother Peter, who in 594 pushed against the Sclaveni north of the Danube and killed the Slav chief Peiragastus at the crossing of the river Helibacias, though his army then suffered from lack of water and a costly ambush. Theophylact presents Peter as incompetent, a view shaped by his sources' loyalty to Priscus.

battle.significance: Kept the Slavs on the defensive north of the river.

events.debate: Whitby dates the campaign to 594; others to 597.

events.title: Gregory of Tours completes the Ten Books of Histories
events.summary: Gregory, bishop of Tours from 573, completed his Decem libri historiarum around 594, the year of his death, carrying the story from Creation to 591. Books 5-10 are an eyewitness record of the civil wars of Chilperic, Guntram, Sigibert and Brunhild. His self-consciously rustic Latin and taste for violent anecdote created the lasting image of Merovingian barbarism.

events.title: Evagrius completes his Ecclesiastical History
events.summary: Evagrius Scholasticus, lawyer to the patriarch Gregory of Antioch, finished his six-book Ecclesiastical History, covering 431 to 594, in Maurice's twelfth year. A Chalcedonian who had survived the plague four times and lost children and grandchildren to it, he preserves documents such as Zeno's Henotikon and the dedications of Khosrow II.

events.title: Avar attack on Singidunum and raid into Dalmatia
events.summary: Angered by Roman campaigns against the Slavs, Bayan attacked Singidunum in 595 and began to dismantle its walls, but withdrew after Priscus's fleet appeared on the Danube. The Avars then invaded Dalmatia, taking Bonkeis and some forty forts, while a Roman force under Guduin could only shadow them.

battle.significance: Avars turned to Dalmatia.

events.title: Avar siege of Tomis and the Easter truce
events.summary: In winter 597-598 the Avars besieged Priscus's army at Tomis. When the Romans ran out of food at Easter, Bayan granted a five-day truce and sent wagons of provisions, an episode Theophylact relates with wonder. Comentiolus then failed to relieve Tomis; the Avars marched to Drizipera near the capital, where plague killed seven of the khagan's sons.

battle.significance: Led to the peace of 598.

events.title: Maurice's testament
events.summary: During an illness in 597 Maurice drafted a will, discovered after his death, dividing the empire between his sons: Theodosius was to rule from Constantinople and Tiberius from Rome over Italy and the islands, with other provinces for the younger sons. It shows that the idea of a resident western emperor was still alive at the end of the sixth century.

events.title: Peace of 598 with the Avars
events.summary: After the plague at Drizipera, Bayan agreed to a treaty raising the annual subsidy by 20,000 solidi, fixing the Danube as the frontier, and allowing the Romans to cross it to campaign against the Sclaveni. Maurice broke it the next year by sending Priscus across at Viminacium.

events.title: Gregory brokers peace between Agilulf and the exarch
events.summary: Pope Gregory, who had already paid Agilulf 500 lb of gold to spare Rome in 593 and had been rebuked by Maurice as a simpleton, finally brought the exarch Callinicus and Agilulf to a truce in 598, renewed in following years. The episode shows the papacy acting as an independent power in Italian diplomacy.

events.title: Plague of 599-600
events.summary: A renewed outbreak of bubonic plague struck Constantinople, Asia Minor, Syria and Italy in 599-600; Theophanes reports great mortality in the capital, and Gregory the Great's letters describe sickness in Italy and Africa. The epidemic had already hit the Avar army at Drizipera in 598.

events.title: Khosrow II ends the Lakhmid kingdom
events.summary: Khosrow II deposed and imprisoned (later killed) al-Nu'man III, the Christian Lakhmid king of al-Hira, around 602 and replaced him with Iyas ibn Qabisa of Tayy and a Persian resident. The end of the Lakhmid buffer, following the Roman break-up of the Ghassanids, removed both empires' Arab shields; the Persian defeat at Dhi Qar soon followed.

events.title: Avar attack on the Antes
events.summary: In 602 the khagan sent his general Apsich to destroy the Antes, a Slavic people east of the Carpathians allied with the Romans. Theophylact notes that many Avars deserted to the emperor during the campaign. It is the last mention of the Antes in the sources.

events.title: Maurice stoned at the Hypapante
events.summary: During a food shortage in February 602, a crowd attacked Maurice with stones during the procession of the Hypapante (Purification); he escaped to the palace with his son Theodosius. The mob then paraded a man resembling the emperor on a donkey, crowned with garlic, chanting insults about his avarice. The Greens' hostility would help Phocas in November.
